Nitra Orthodox Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Nitra, Slovakia

Not demolished. This cemetery served Nitra's Orthodox congregation, which formed after the 1868-69 Budapest Congress schism split the city's historic Jewish community (first documented in 1113) into separate Orthodox and Neolog streams, each maintaining its own synagogue and cemetery. Nitra was home to Rabbi Samuel Ungar's renowned yeshiva, one of the last operating in Nazi-occupied Europe before its 1944 closure; the city's roughly 4,358 Jews in 1940 were mostly murdered in the Holocaust. About 600 survivors returned after the war, reorganizing as a single Orthodox community and restoring this and the adjoining Neolog cemetery, adding a Holocaust memorial. In 1963, authorities destroyed most of Nitra's Jewish public buildings except the Neolog synagogue; the cemeteries were vandalized with swastikas again after 1989. Some sources describe an older site established in 1899, with burials continuing until Nitra's Jewish religious community formally ceased operating in 1965.
